title: Recursive CTEs
objective: Write WITH RECURSIVE queries to generate sequences (numbers, days, months) and walk hierarchies (category trees) to get depth, paths and all descendants.
context: Two everyday problems need recursion. First, reports must show every month, including months with zero revenue, so you need a calendar (a 'spine') to LEFT JOIN onto. Second, the category tree (All Products → Electronics → Audio) has unknown depth, so a fixed number of self-joins won't do.

exercises.title: Count from 1 to 12
exercises.question: You need a helper list of month numbers 1–12 for a report template.
exercises.prompt: Using a recursive CTE (no tables needed), return one column month_number with the integers 1 through 12.
hints: Anchor: SELECT 1. Recursive step: previous value + 1.
The stop condition goes in the recursive part's WHERE.
WITH RECURSIVE nums(month_number) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT month_number + 1 FROM nums WHERE month_number < 12) SELECT month_number FROM nums;
exercises.why: Number generators are the building block of every spine, bucket list and test-data generator.

recall.q: What happens if a recursive CTE has no stop condition?
recall.a: It recurses forever (or until the engine's recursion limit errors out).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) AS month_number FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 12));

exercises.title: Category depth
exercises.question: The site team needs each category's depth in the navigation tree.
exercises.prompt: Return category_id, category_name and depth for all 14 categories, where the root ('All Products', parent NULL) has depth 0, its children depth 1, and so on.
hints: Anchor: the root, WHERE parent_category_id IS NULL, with depth 0.
Recursive step: categories whose parent is a row already in the CTE; depth = parent's depth + 1.
... UNION ALL SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name, t.depth + 1 FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_category_id = t.category_id
exercises.why: Depth drives indentation in menus and lets you report 'at level 1' consistently, however deep the tree grows. Strength Training sits at depth 3.

recall.q: In a parent→child tree walk, what does the recursive JOIN condition look like?
recall.a: child.parent_id = cte.id (find rows whose parent was found in the previous step).

exercises.title: Breadcrumb paths
exercises.question: The website needs breadcrumb text like 'All Products > Sports > Fitness'.
exercises.prompt: Return category_id and path for all 14 categories, where path is the chain of category names from the root down to that category joined with ' > ' (the root's path is just 'All Products'). Sort by path.
hints: Carry a text column through the recursion and extend it at each step.
Recursive part: t.path || ' > ' || c.category_name
Anchor: SELECT category_id, category_name AS path FROM categories WHERE parent_category_id IS NULL; finish with ORDER BY path.
exercises.why: Paths make hierarchies readable in flat reports, and sorting by path lists every category directly under its parent: a tree view for free.

recall.q: How do you build a path string in a recursive CTE?
recall.a: Carry it as a column: anchor = root name; step = parent_path || ' > ' || child_name.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT category_id, SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(category_name, ' > ') FROM categories START WITH parent_category_id IS NULL CONNECT BY PRIOR category_id = parent_category_id; (path starts with the separator).

exercises.title: Everything under Electronics
exercises.question: A promotion applies to 'Electronics and all its sub-categories'. Which categories are in scope?
exercises.prompt: Return category_id, category_name for 'Electronics' itself and all of its descendants (children, grandchildren, ...). Start the anchor from the name 'Electronics', not a hard-coded id.
hints: Same tree walk, but the anchor is the Electronics row instead of the root.
Anchor: WHERE category_name = 'Electronics'.

WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (SELECT ... WHERE category_name = 'Electronics' UNION ALL SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name FROM categories c JOIN sub s ON c.parent_category_id = s.category_id) SELECT ... FROM sub;
exercises.why: 'X and everything below it' is the standard question for org charts, product trees and geographies. Recursion keeps working when someone adds a sub-sub-category next quarter.

recall.q: How do you change a full-tree walk into a 'subtree of X' walk?
recall.a: Change the anchor to select X instead of the root.

exercises.title: Descendant counts for every category
exercises.question: Navigation design wants to know how many categories sit beneath each node (at any depth).
exercises.prompt: Return category_id, category_name and descendant_count (the number of categories strictly below it at any depth; 0 for leaves) for all 14 categories.
hints: Build (ancestor_id, descendant_id) pairs: anchor = every direct parent/child pair.
Recursive step: extend each pair one level down: join categories whose parent is the pair's descendant, keeping the ancestor.
Then LEFT JOIN categories to the pairs on ancestor_id and COUNT(descendant_id) (leaves get 0).
exercises.why: An ancestor/descendant 'closure table' answers every roll-up question about a hierarchy (counts, revenue under a node) with an ordinary join and GROUP BY.

recall.a: A table of every (ancestor, descendant) pair in a hierarchy, at any distance.

exercises.title: Monthly Books revenue with zero months
exercises.question: The Books manager's chart skips months with no sales, which makes the trend look better than it is.
exercises.prompt: Generate every month from 2024-01 to 2025-12 with a recursive CTE, then return month ('YYYY-MM') and books_revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) for products with category 'Books' on valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), rounded to 2 decimals, showing 0 for months without Books sales. Sort by month.
hints: Spine: anchor date('2024-01-01'), step date(month_start, '+1 month'), stop at '2025-12-01'.
Aggregate Books revenue per 'YYYY-MM' in a second CTE (you can list it after the recursive one).
FROM months m LEFT JOIN books_monthly b ON b.month = strftime('%Y-%m', m.month_start), COALESCE(b.revenue, 0), ORDER BY month.
exercises.why: Eight of the 24 months have no Books sales. Without a spine they vanish from the chart and any moving average or month-over-month calculation silently skips them.

recall.q: Why LEFT JOIN facts onto a date spine instead of grouping the facts alone?
recall.a: Grouping facts only produces months that have data; the spine guarantees every month appears (with 0).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT DATEADD('month', ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) - 1, '2024-01-01'::date) AS month_start FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 24)); then LEFT JOIN on DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) = month_start.

exercises.title: Daily orders in December 2025
exercises.question: Ops wants a day-by-day order count for December 2025, including the quiet days.
exercises.prompt: Generate every day from 2025-12-01 to 2025-12-31 and return order_day ('YYYY-MM-DD') and orders_placed (number of orders of any status with that order_date, 0 if none). Sort by order_day.
hints: Same spine pattern with '+1 day'.
LEFT JOIN orders on order_date = order_day and COUNT(o.order_id), not COUNT(*).

WITH RECURSIVE days(order_day) AS (SELECT date('2025-12-01') UNION ALL SELECT date(order_day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE order_day < '2025-12-31') SELECT d.order_day, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_placed FROM days d LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date = d.order_day GROUP BY d.order_day ORDER BY d.order_day;
exercises.why: Only 3 of 31 days have orders. Daily spines are what make 'orders per day' averages honest (3/31, not 3/3).

recall.q: After a LEFT JOIN onto a spine, why COUNT(o.order_id) and not COUNT(*)?
recall.a: COUNT(*) would count the NULL-extended row on empty days as 1; COUNT(column) gives 0.

worked_example.question: List the direct and indirect sub-categories of 'Home', with their depth below Home.
worked_example.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
    SELECT category_id, category_name, 0 AS levels_below
    FROM categories
    WHERE category_name = 'Home'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name, s.levels_below + 1
    FROM categories AS c
    JOIN sub AS s ON c.parent_category_id = s.category_id
)
SELECT * FROM sub;
worked_example.explanation: The anchor finds Home. Each recursive pass finds the children of the rows found in the previous pass (Kitchen, Decor). When a pass finds no new rows, recursion stops on its own, because a finite tree is its own stop condition.

recipe:
**Recipe: anchor + recursive step + stop condition**

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE seq(n) AS (
    SELECT 1                 -- 1. anchor: the starting row(s)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM seq    -- 2. recursive step: build the next row from the previous one
    WHERE n < 10             -- 3. stop condition: without it the query never ends
)
SELECT n FROM seq;
```

**Walking a tree (parent → children):**
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT category_id, category_name, 0 AS depth, category_name AS path
    FROM categories WHERE parent_category_id IS NULL                  -- root(s)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name, t.depth + 1, t.path || ' > ' || c.category_name
    FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_category_id = t.category_id   -- children of rows found so far
)
SELECT * FROM tree;
```

**Date spine:** anchor `SELECT date('2024-01-01') AS month_start`, step `date(month_start, '+1 month')`,
stop `WHERE month_start < '2025-12-01'`. Then `spine LEFT JOIN facts` + `COALESCE(revenue, 0)`.

Rules: anchor and recursive parts are joined with `UNION ALL`; the recursive part references the CTE **once**;
always have a stop condition (or a depth limit to defend against cycles).
snowflake_notes:
- Snowflake accepts `WITH RECURSIVE` (the RECURSIVE keyword is optional there). It also has the Oracle-style
  `CONNECT BY PRIOR category_id = parent_category_id START WITH parent_category_id IS NULL`, with
  `SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(category_name, ' > ')` and `LEVEL`.
- For number/date spines Snowflake developers usually skip recursion:
  `SELECT DATEADD('month', SEQ4(), '2024-01-01'::date) AS month_start FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 24))`.
  (Note SEQ4 can have gaps in theory; `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) - 1` is the safe version.)
- `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)` replaces SQLite's `date(order_date, 'start of month')`.
common_mistakes: Missing or wrong stop condition: infinite recursion (or a spine one month too long/short; check the endpoints).
Using UNION instead of UNION ALL in the recursive CTE. It is allowed in SQLite but slower, and hides cycle bugs.
Reversing the tree join (c.category_id = t.parent_category_id walks *up* the tree, not down).
Joining facts to the spine with a mismatched key format ('2024-01-01' vs '2024-01'). Format both sides the same way.
COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(fact_column) after a LEFT JOIN onto a spine: empty periods show 1 instead of 0.
recall: What are the three parts of a recursive CTE?
Anchor member, recursive member (referencing the CTE), and a stop condition; joined with UNION ALL.
How do you make empty months appear with 0 revenue?
Generate a month spine, LEFT JOIN the aggregated facts to it, COALESCE(revenue, 0).
How do you defend against cycles in hierarchical data?
Carry a depth (or path) column and stop at a maximum depth / when the id already appears in the path.
